Okay I coined a phrase. 

AI mysticism. 

I define AI mysticism as the idea that calculating machines that can do perhaps trillions of times more than what computers did in earlier decades as waking up somehow just from the fact that they got a lot of signals being traded between bits of circuits. The idea that they can do stuff that maybe makes a lot of people wonder is something that could cause them to wake up become conscious and then realize that they are superior to us in some ways are always. 

My take on all this, relates to when I first got a four function calculator back in 1975 that could take four five combinations of numbers I could multiply them add them and then divide them again and press buttons and this thing would do things that I could not do even in a full day with pen and paper and this thing could take the and do it absolutely 100% accurate at least up to about seven digits or something in that order. 

Open AI gave us chat GPT which is one of the greatest word complete programs ever and it's kind of like my little handheld calculator taken to 10 of the 12th power or so. These are calculators not thinking beings. I wonder if it's more dangerous to mystify AI than it is to essentially basically classify it what it actually is and that is exceedingly powerful calculating machines and they are extremely useful tools. They are not conscious they probably will never be conscious however they might essentially be intelligent in many ways that we are not but that's not the same as being a living being with a brain and will. 

However there is no doubt that the wrong people was sufficiently powerful computing systems are pretty dangerous though so we need to control for that.

comments.author: @starbock
comments.text:
@WesRoth - I generally like and appreciate your reporting, including this installment.  And, as you appear to have, too, I have growing concerns about what feels like cultish mindset from EA, so please do not misinterpret my view.

That said, @10:00 you said, "By the way, me personally, I'm never surprised that some of these high-charging people aren't 'nice.' I think deep down to go that hard after some of these goals you kind of have to be a bit of a killer. Look at Steve Jobs ..."

It's views and statements like these that normalize what is not normal.  No, you don't need to be an a-hole to do great things in this world.  And, as long as we expect that is necessary, that is exactly the type of "leadership" that we will continue to have.

It is not normal for companies to exhibit the behaviors that are common in today's corporate world.  It is not normal for people to feel abused, exploited, belittled, etc. no matter what lofty goal there may be - the end does not justify the means.

I agree with inspiring people to be a better self than they are today, absolutely.  Keyword is inspire, which is not what happens in the majority of "high-charging people" scenarios - inclusive of all the ones that you referenced.

And, this is precisely why I believe that we need to be extra careful where AI is concerned, and why we need to apply higher-than-normal standards vs lower the bar as far as we need to get "there."  AI is a magnifier of human capability.  We need to be careful what we magnify.  And, if there are reasons for concern about the people leading and building AI ... that needs to be addressed before it's too late.

I don't know Sam Altman.  What I do know is that where there is smoke there is fire.  Whether it's a smoldering match or a nuclear detonation, I do not know.  We should all know - THAT is what needs to be OPEN about OpenAI.  🙏

comments.author: @derasor
comments.text:
My 2 cents are that right now LLMs do have impressive abilities saving up time in routine tasks that need consolidating existing knowledge. That is IMO a ‘general’ skill that requires some form of actual understanding and introspection (not ‘consciousness’). And if we believe the whale analogy, these agents could become a lot better than what they are now, but both data and compute have very real, and multifaceted, limits. Now if you look at the ‘narrow’ AI of the sort of AlphaFold, (specialized in this biology task of finding form for biomolecules (proteins), that now is tackling interactions in the next upgrades) a so called ‘general’ agent, not even the whale, could compete in this specific task with the specialized system… they could be used (the general ones) to improve specific aspects of the specialized system, and event o design new ones that perform better than the original ones, but this is far from the so called ‘intelligence explosion’ most people seem to have accepted as fact. If you look at a precedent, the AlphaGo Zero reached what by all accounts could be interpreted as maxed out performance, Go is solved, end of the story. Intelligence is not a scale but a medium and once a solution is found, more intelligence (all the way to infinite, whatever that means) doesn’t make any difference. If we want to, say, solve biology, we need a specialized system build with the help of multiple, highly capable, general agents, and then (hopefully) is, de-facto, solved (our understanding of it at least). Same for physics, chemistry, materials, propulsion, energy, etc (de-facto, cuz mAxImUm tRuTh sEeKiNg is not a thing given the limits of provability in formal axiomatic theories... see Gödel).... And then, having a solution (in knowledge) and building actual stuff on top of it are VERY different things. Besides, the agents will not be human even if scale allows them to have their own sense of ‘consciousness’ as some sort of emergent property, but even this will not be in operation beyond their hardware run. They can not be plotting and scheming a take-over if they are not prompted to do so, because they can only be doing linear algebra with the prompt on a given inference. Now, if the prompts are jailbreaking attempts, that is another issue, originated from the human user, not from the system itself. And that surely needs to be taken care of somehow but this is not adversarial to the nature, of the existence, of the agent (the hardware computing matrix operations) 

Also, Dr. LeCun is right about pointing out how this subconscious bias, planted by ‘ultra-religious’ upbringing, plays a big role in the discourse of doomers, and the reach that they have with the broader audience. Maybe even plain religious dogmas are enough to form these cognitive dissonances in the human mind, and have these unreasonable collateral narratives end up having way more attention, and consequences (like overshadowing actual pressing real-time concerns), that they should ever have. For all their defense of rationality, these beliefs in extreme outcomes makes these people a de facto religion, and in religion doubt is not permitted, and faith trumps critical thinking.

comments.text:
I think your position is mostly emotional. You are wary of the EA movement, you don’t trust Helen because of her connection to it, and this causes you to be suspicious of taking anything she says at face value. Even your reaction to the question about whether it’s reasonable or rational to enter nuclear war is based on your internal feeling of how reasonable it sounds. I totally agree that it doesn’t sound reasonable to me either, but that’s just how I feel about it.

The interesting thing about all of this is that Yudkowsky is using a practical technique to calculate probabilities under uncertainty. To him, Bayesian logic is kind of the ultimate outcome predictor. He’s done his best to use it appropriately, and to him, the probabilistic outcome is that AI will destroy us.

Now imagine being so sure of the logic and math that the answer seems completely obvious and inescapable — almost like it’s screaming in your face. 

Now look, I’m just a “normie.” I barely understand Bayesian logic at all, and I have no idea if he’s applying it correctly. But from his point of view, the data is screaming in his face that AI will certainly kill us. From that perspective, his opinions are completely rational and reasonable. If AI will certainly destroy us, then it’s imperative for the survival of the species that we take every possible measure all the way up to and including nuclear war to prevent it. If AI spells certain doom, then every action with less certainty of doom is on the table.

I’m not here to defend EA or anything. I’m just saying that there are issues with the information as you are presenting it. I think it’s more accurate to say that EA people have run calculations that they believe are telling them that AI will certainly destroy us. And therefore, their behavior reflects the urgency and seriousness of that position of belief. We should continue to see EA types of people pushing for AI bans and shutdowns, but while they have billions of dollars to try and make that happen, so do large corporations with profit interest in the tech. EA is not likely going to win.

comments.text: Yudkowsky's opinion is on the extreme end of things - but whether he's right or wrong, AI alignment, isn't exactly being taken seriously is it? There should be some sort of independent regulatory oversight to ensure that a few individuals who don't take risks with the future of humanity - this is not about being a doomer, but about managing risk.
